title: Schumer Vows Democrats Will Block Any Right-Winger Trump Supreme Court Nominee
excerpt: Two days after winning a decisive Senate majority, Chuck Schumer told the Associated Press Democrats will reject far-right nominees for the Supreme Court, lower courts and Cabinet — while refusing to say if he would hold a vacancy open until after the next presidential election.
body:
• Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Democrats will not allow President Donald Trump to put “a right-winger” on the Supreme Court once they take power.
  • Schumer said the party will also reject what he called “crappy nominees” for lower courts and Cabinet posts.
  • He declined to say whether he would hold a vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as Mitch McConnell did in 2016.
  • Democrats could hold as many as 56 Senate seats if they win still-uncalled races in Mississippi and Alaska, according to the AP report.

WASHINGTON — Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is vowing that Democrats will not allow President Donald Trump to put “a right-winger” on the Supreme Court once they take power, raising the possibility that his party could block a presidential nominee if a vacancy arises in the next two years.

“The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” Schumer said in an interview with The Associated Press on Thursday, reported by The Washington Sun and NewsLooks.

A pledge with no vacancy yet

There is currently no vacancy on the high court, and Schumer’s comments were about how Democrats would respond if one arises. He would not say whether he would hold a vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as former Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016.

But he was explicit about the standard he intends to apply. Democrats are “not going to allow any crappy nominees” to be confirmed to the Supreme Court — or to the lower courts or Trump’s Cabinet, either, he said.

With control of the Senate, Democrats would control committees and the confirmation process, giving them the power to reject Trump’s choices and press him toward more moderate nominees.

"Democrats are “not going to allow any crappy nominees” to be confirmed to the Supreme Court — or to the lower courts or Trump’s Cabinet, either, he said."

Two days after a decisive majority

Schumer’s pledge came two days after Democrats won a decisive Senate majority in the midterm elections — a result few predicted a year ago, when Schumer faced intense criticism from progressives and Senate Republicans were betting a favorable map and backing from Trump would help them keep power.

Democrats could have as many as 56 seats if they win Mississippi and Alaska, which had still not been called. Schumer described that as “a durable majority,” 20 years in the making, and predicted “it’s not just a flip of the Senate once.”

He is expected to be reelected as leader by his caucus after leading Democrats to wins in Republican-leaning states. He is up for reelection in 2028 and would not say whether he will seek a sixth term. “I’m focused on 2027,” he said.

Costs, oversight and the limits of divided government

Beyond nominations, Schumer said the party’s agenda will center on lowering prices, along with healthcare, housing, Trump’s tariffs, childcare and lowering energy bills. Democrats also want to investigate Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids and scrutinize the Trump administration, which he called the “most corrupted administration by far in American history.”

He also said the majority could halt the Iran war and alter policies Democrats were unable to counter in the minority. On process, however, he left key questions open: he would not say whether he would try to eliminate the filibuster, which he tried and failed to change when he was majority leader during President Joe Biden’s term, to allow legislation to pass with a simple majority instead of 60 votes.

“The focus has got to be on getting things done,” he said. “That’s all I am saying.”

Asked whether he would support a third Trump impeachment, Schumer said he would support an impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, an effort House lawmakers have already launched. On Trump himself, he said: “That’s up to the House.”

Why it matters beyond Washington

For Indian American readers, Senate control over confirmations shapes the federal courts that decide immigration, employment and civil-rights cases, as well as the Cabinet officials who run the agencies diaspora families deal with. No nominee has been named and no seat is open, so the immediate effect is leverage: any future Trump pick for the courts or Cabinet will now have to clear a Senate led by a leader who has publicly ruled out a far-right choice.
